For each scenario below, predict whether React PRESERVES the component instance (state kept) or REMOUNTS it (state destroyed), with a one-line reason. The solution logs all six predictions.

1. `<div>` → `<span>` at the same position
2. `<Counter count={1} />` → `<Counter count={2} />`

```bash
node solution.js
```

Expected output (exactly):

```

   PREDICT: REMOUNT — different element type, React tears down the whole subtree
2. <Counter count={1} /> -> <Counter count={2} />
   PREDICT: PRESERVE — same type at same position, React updates props and keeps state
3. {editing ? <EditForm/> : <Preview/>} toggled

4. {show ? <Panel/> : null} toggled off and on

```

lessons.body:
## The problem React refused to solve

Diffing two trees to find the minimal set of edits is O(n^3) in the general case. At 60fps, with trees thousands of nodes deep, that is not a trade-off — it is a non-starter. So React cheated: it replaced the general problem with a simpler one, using two heuristics that hold true for virtually all real UIs.

## Heuristic 1: different types mean different trees

If the element type changes at a position — `<div>` becomes `<span>`, or `<Counter>` becomes `<Timer>` — React does not diff. It tears down the old subtree (unmounting everything, destroying state) and builds the new one from scratch.

## Heuristic 2: keys hint at stable identity

For lists, the `key` prop tells React which child in the new render corresponds to which child in the old one, even when order changes. Keys are how the O(n) pass survives reordering.

## The O(n) pass

With those assumptions, reconciliation becomes a single level-by-level walk, comparing children pairwise by position:

- Same type at the same position → keep the DOM node, diff the props, recurse into children.
- Different type → replace the whole subtree.
- Keyed children → match by key first, then apply the same rules (this is where moves come from).

## Why this matters for interviews

When an interviewer asks "how does React update the DOM?", they want the heuristics, the O(n) complexity, and the consequence: React's correctness depends on type-and-position identity, and keys are the escape hatch you control. Everything in the next three lessons is a consequence of this design.
keyPoints: General tree diffing is O(n^3); React's heuristics make it O(n).
Different element type at the same position → full subtree teardown and remount.
Same type → keep the DOM node, diff props, recurse into children pairwise.
Keys let the diff match children across renders even when order changes.
lessons.title: The Diffing Heuristics

lessons.body:
## Identity is type plus position

Every element in React's tree has an identity, and React computes it from two things: the element's **type** and its **position** among siblings. Same type at the same position across renders → same identity → the component instance (and its state) is preserved. Change either one and React treats it as something new.

## The classic state-loss bug

```jsx
{isEditing ? <EditForm draft={draft} /> : <Preview draft={draft} />}
```

Toggling `isEditing` swaps the component type at that position. React unmounts `EditForm` — destroying its state — and mounts `Preview` fresh. Toggle back and the form state is gone. This is not a bug in React; it is the heuristic working as designed.

## Fixes, in order of preference

- Render one component and vary its behavior with props: `<Form mode={isEditing ? "edit" : "preview"} />`. Same type, same position → state preserved.
- If the two branches must be different components, keep both mounted and toggle visibility with CSS.
- Reach for `key` only when you *want* the remount (see the reset pattern in the keys lesson).

## Position shifts remount too

Wrapping a subtree in an extra `<div>` — even conditionally — changes every child's position and can remount the whole subtree. Conditional wrappers are one of the most common accidental-remount sources in production codebases.

## The interview one-liner

"React preserves state by identity, and identity is type plus position unless a key says otherwise."
keyPoints: Element identity = type + position; a key overrides the position part.
Swapping component types in a ternary unmounts and remounts — state is destroyed.
Prefer one component with a mode prop over two components in a conditional.
Conditional wrapper elements shift positions and can remount entire subtrees.
lessons.title: Element Identity: Preserve vs Remount

lessons.body:
## What keys are for

Keys answer one question across renders: *which child is which?* When a list re-renders, React matches old children to new children by key, then applies the normal rules — same key and type means the instance (and its state) survives a move.

## Why index keys break

Array indices are stable only when the list never reorders, filters, or inserts. The moment it does, React matches by position and the component instances — with their state, focus, input values, and animation progress — stay glued to the *position* instead of following the *item*.

The canonical production bug: a list of inputs keyed by index. Insert a row at the top and every input's text appears to shift down one row. Nothing "moved" in the data — the DOM nodes stayed put while the items slid underneath them.

## Rules that survive contact with production

- Use stable, unique IDs from your data. Database IDs are ideal.
- Keys only need to be unique among siblings, not globally.
- Never generate keys during render (`key={Math.random()}` or `key={uuid()}` inline): a new key every render means a remount every render.
- Generate the ID once, when the item is created, and store it with the data.

## The legitimate key abuse

`key` is also a deliberate remount switch. `<ProfileForm key={userId} />` resets all form state when the user changes — no manual reset logic, no stale state. When you *want* a fresh instance, changing the key is the cleanest way to say so.
keyPoints: Keys match children across renders; instances and state follow the key.
Index keys glue state to position — reordering, filtering, or inserting breaks them.
Generate stable IDs once at item creation; never during render.
Changing a key on purpose is the cleanest way to force a state reset.
lessons.title: Keys Done Right

lessons.body:
## Fragments `<>` (or ``) groups children without adding a DOM node — useful when a wrapper would break layout or shift positions. One catch: the shorthand cannot take a key. For keyed groups, use the explicit form: ```jsx {sections.map((s) => (

{s.title}

{s.body}

 ))} ``` ## Conditional rendering unmounts `{show && }` renders nothing when `show` is false — React unmounts `Panel`. Toggling it back is a fresh mount: state lost, effects re-run, data refetched. If the panel is expensive or stateful and toggled often, keeping it mounted and hiding it with CSS can be the better trade. ## Same position, different type This is the identity rule applied to ternaries: `{tab === "a" ? : }` remounts on every tab switch. If the panes hold draft state, lift it above the ternary or unify the component. ## Keys at every array level Nested arrays need keys at each level — the inner `.map()` included. A missing key deep in the tree produces the same position-glued bugs, just harder to find. ## The two-second key audit For every list, ask: "can this list ever reorder, filter, or have items inserted?" If yes — and in production the answer is almost always yes eventually — it needs stable keys.
keyPoints: Fragments group without DOM nodes; only <Fragment> (not <>) accepts a key.
Conditional rendering unmounts — toggling back is a fresh mount with fresh state.
Ternaries switching component types remount on every toggle; lift state above them.
Nested .map() calls need keys at every level.
